promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 5 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: Last week went exactly to plan, so next week grows about 10 percent to 44 miles on your usual five days. Doubling to 80 would add injury risk that will not turn into fitness before the race.

answers.question: My club mate runs 70 miles a week before a marathon. I'm thinking of doubling to 80 next week to catch up, running twice a day. Would that work?
answers.answer:
No. Going to 80 miles would double last week's 40 and is the quickest way to start the race hurt or flat.

Your last four weeks show how much you have already ramped:

| Week | Miles |
| --- | --- |
| Aug 24 – 30 | 27 |
| Aug 31 – Sep 6 | 37 |
| Sep 7 – 13 | 53 |
| Sep 14 – 20 | 40 |

The 53-mile week, with the 20-mile long run, already left your calves tight and your legs heavy early the next week. Eighty miles would be about half as much again on top of that peak.

Catching up does not work this close to the race. Training takes a few weeks to turn into fitness, so miles added now will not pay off by Nov 1, but the fatigue and injury risk will. Your club mate's 70 sits on a long, gradual build.

You are not behind. Six miles at 8:30 to 8:40 per mile on Wednesday is right on 3:45 pace, and your long run held steady with no fade. Next week goes to 44 miles on your usual five days, with no second runs in a day. After that, add no more than about 10 percent a week, and put the extra into the long run and easy days.

new.analysis:
Last week followed the plan, and that is the main reason it went well. Every run matched its planned distance within a tenth of a mile, both rest days stayed rest days, and nothing extra was added. That is the opposite of the week of Sep 7 – 13, when you ran 53 miles against a planned 38 and added a fourth rep and a 20-mile long run.

The cost of that overrun showed up in your own notes. Calves were tight on the Sunday night, and legs felt heavy early in the following week before clearing by Thursday. You got away with it, but it is the mild version of what a much bigger jump would cost.

The marathon-pace work is on target. The 6 miles on Wednesday held 8:30 to 8:40 per mile against 8:35 for a 3:45 finish, at effort 7/10. Holding that for 26.2 miles is a bigger job, so the next step is to practise it inside a long run, when your legs are already tired.

That is why the long run now carries a marathon-pace stretch and Wednesday goes back to threshold work. The two quality sessions sit well apart, which fits your five-day week and keeps the other three runs easy. Seventeen miles is about 2 h 45 min at your pace, inside the 2.5 to 3 hours that does the job, so there is no need to chase another 20.

Total mileage rises by about 10 percent, which is a step your body has already shown it can absorb. The extra comes from a longer run in the middle of the week and a slightly longer long run, not from extra days or doubles.

Your easy-running share was 64 percent against the 80 percent target. With a quality session and a long run in the week that is expected, and your easy runs sat steady at 139 bpm. Most of the gap came from the long run, where heart rate climbed from 143 to 152 and about 55 percent of the time was in zone 3, so a slightly slower start keeps it honest.

Two more build weeks follow this one, the weeks of Sep 28 and Oct 5. I expect the taper to start the week of Oct 12, so these are the last weeks to add load.
